title: Foreboding in teaching
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino starts from a small domestic moment, fixating on a spilled-cereal risk instead of listening to her son, to examine how teachers anticipate trouble. She argues that predicting problems from experience is natural and necessary, but that dread by itself distorts attention. The examples are a difficult class arriving, speaking in front of colleagues and meeting a line manager. Her move is to separate foreboding from planning: each worry should be turned into a concrete plan for preventing or handling the event. Where a teacher lacks the experience to predict what may happen, she recommends seeking out those who have it, including through blogs, Twitter and knowledge-based professional networks. The result is a short, personal piece on teacher anxiety and professional habits.
points: Anticipating poor behaviour is necessary, and starting fresh with a class does not mean ignoring its history.
The key distinction is between dreading an event and holding a plan to prevent or handle it.
Early-career anxiety often reflects missing experience, which can be borrowed from more experienced colleagues.
Knowledge-based professional networks help teachers see out-of-control situations from other viewpoints.
Having a plan frees attention to focus on what is actually happening instead of the feared event.
quotes: Looking at the first example from the list above, if we don’t predict the potential for poor behaviour with some classes, then chaos can ensue. Starting fresh each time does not mean ignoring past behaviour. It means we need to prevent past behaviours from resurging in our classroom (or stopping behaviour starting, as Adam Boxer so eloquently puts it).

As with my son, I find that sometimes these anxieties take over my thought-process and I focus less on what is actually being said. But, at the same time, the situations in the list above are not exactly ‘bad’.

It is all well and good to say “have a plan” but how do we plan for things when sometimes we may not have the answer? I felt like this when I was an NQT. I didn’t have much teaching experience, I had a few tricky classes, and I was anxious about everything.

Now, if you are like me and shy away from actually talking to people (at least, initially), Twitter, reading and writing blogs have helped massively. Luckily for us, people write and discuss all sorts of topics.

Of course, in some cases, there are various factors causing anxiety and a sense of foreboding. Being a part of a knowledge-based professional netwrok can help us evaluate situations from a different view-point, especially if discussing things we feel are out of our control.

In summary, being able to predict negative events is a good thing, but having a plan for how to prevent or deal with them is even better. Doing so means we can focus more on other things and not solely on the event.
